sentence: The committee will ___ a decision next week.
explanation: make a decision is the fixed collocation; we do not 'do' or 'give' a decision.

sentence: She has ___ great progress since she changed schools.
explanation: make progress is the collocation; after 'has' the past participle 'made' is needed.

sentence: It's hard to ___ friends when you move to a new city.
explanation: make friends is the fixed expression for forming friendships.

sentence: Could you ___ me a favour and close the window?
explanation: do somebody a favour is the fixed collocation; 'make a favour' is a common error.

sentence: The scientists are ___ research into new forms of energy.
explanation: do research (into something) is the collocation; 'make research' is wrong.

sentence: Smoking can ___ serious harm to your health.
explanation: do harm to something is the fixed phrase; 'make harm' is a common learner error.

sentence: They ___ a lot of business with companies in Asia.
explanation: do business with somebody is the fixed expression for commercial activity.

sentence: We ___ our shopping at the local market every Saturday.
explanation: do the shopping is the collocation for buying food and household goods.

sentence: She ___ very well in her end-of-year exams.
hint: collocation: to ___ well in an exam
explanation: do well in an exam is the standard phrase meaning to perform successfully.

sentence: We were asked to ___ an experiment in the laboratory.
explanation: do an experiment is the standard collocation in scientific contexts.

sentence: I must ___ my homework before I can go out.
explanation: do homework is the fixed collocation; 'make homework' is a common learner error.

sentence: The storm ___ a lot of damage to the roof.
explanation: do damage to something is the collocation; past tense 'did' is needed here.

sentence: He was exhausted because he had ___ the cooking for twenty people.
explanation: do the cooking is the fixed phrase; after 'had' the past participle 'done' is needed.

sentence: Who ___ the washing-up in your house?
explanation: do the washing-up means to wash the dishes; the -s form is needed with 'who'.

sentence: We should ___ an effort to arrive on time.
explanation: make an effort is the fixed collocation meaning to try hard.

sentence: The manager ___ an announcement about the changes yesterday.
explanation: make an announcement is the fixed collocation for stating something publicly.

sentence: I'd like to ___ a suggestion, if I may.
explanation: make a suggestion is the fixed collocation; 'say a suggestion' is not used.

sentence: Her company ___ a huge profit last year.
explanation: make a profit (or make a loss) is the fixed business collocation.

sentence: The children were told not to ___ so much noise.
explanation: make a noise / make noise is the fixed collocation.

sentence: Can we ___ a phone call before we leave?
explanation: make a phone call / make a call is the standard collocation.

sentence: Please ___ sure that all the windows are locked.
explanation: make sure means to check that something is true or has been done.

sentence: We are still ___ arrangements for the wedding.
explanation: make arrangements is the fixed collocation for organising plans.

sentence: He ___ a fortune selling software online.
explanation: make a fortune means to earn a very large amount of money.

sentence: It took her years to ___ a living from her painting.
explanation: make a living means to earn enough money to live on.

sentence: She always ___ her best, even in friendly matches.
explanation: do one's best means to try as hard as possible; the -es form agrees with 'she'.

sentence: I'm ___ a course in web design this term.
explanation: do a course is the British English collocation for studying on a course.

sentence: He ___ some ridiculous excuse about his car breaking down.
explanation: make an excuse is the fixed collocation; 'tell an excuse' is not used.

sentence: We ___ breakfast on the terrace every morning in summer.
explanation: have breakfast/lunch/dinner is the standard collocation for eating meals.

sentence: She ___ a quick shower before leaving the gym.
explanation: have a shower is the standard British English collocation; 'made a shower' is wrong.

sentence: Let's ___ a rest before we continue.
explanation: have a rest is the fixed collocation for pausing to relax.

sentence: The children ___ great fun at the party.
explanation: have fun / have great fun is the fixed collocation; 'made fun' means mocked someone.

sentence: He ___ a serious accident on his motorbike last year.
explanation: have an accident is the fixed collocation for being involved in one.

sentence: I ___ a strange dream last night.
explanation: have a dream is the English collocation; 'see a dream' is a common learner error.

sentence: The neighbours ___ a loud argument in the garden last night.
explanation: have an argument (with somebody) is the fixed collocation for quarrelling.

sentence: We stopped at a cafe to ___ a chat.
explanation: have a chat is the fixed collocation for a friendly, informal conversation.

sentence: Why don't we ___ lunch together on Friday?
explanation: have lunch is the standard collocation for eating lunch.

sentence: She ___ no difficulty finding the address.
hint: fixed pattern: ___ no difficulty doing something
explanation: have no difficulty (in) doing something is the fixed pattern; 'made no difficulty' is wrong.

sentence: Let me ___ a photo of you both.
explanation: take a photo/picture is the fixed collocation for photographing something.

sentence: All candidates must ___ the written exam in June.
hint: collocation with 'exam' from the candidate's side
explanation: take an exam (or sit an exam) means to be tested; 'give an exam' is not used in British English.

sentence: Over five hundred athletes will ___ part in the games.
explanation: take part in something means to participate in it.

sentence: Who will ___ responsibility for the project now that Jane has left?
explanation: take responsibility for something means to accept the duty of dealing with it.

sentence: The wedding will ___ place in the village church.
explanation: take place means to happen; it is the fixed phrase for events.

sentence: Let me ___ a look at that cut on your arm.
explanation: take a look (at something) is the fixed collocation for examining something briefly.

sentence: We ___ a taxi from the airport because it was raining.
explanation: take a taxi/bus/train is the standard collocation for using transport.

sentence: She ___ great pride in her grandchildren's achievements.
explanation: take pride in something means to be pleased and satisfied with it.

sentence: You are ___ a big risk if you invest all your money in one company.
explanation: take a risk means to do something that might have a bad result.

sentence: I would never ___ advice from someone I don't respect.
hint: collocation with 'advice' from the receiver's side
explanation: take advice from somebody means to accept and follow it; the adviser gives advice.

sentence: Please ___ your seats; the performance is about to begin.
explanation: take your seats is the formal way of asking people to sit down.

sentence: Let's ___ a break and continue after lunch.
explanation: take a break is the fixed collocation for pausing work or activity.

sentence: Students should ___ notes while they listen to the lecture.
explanation: take notes is the standard collocation for writing down information.

sentence: He didn't ___ any interest in politics until university.
explanation: take an interest in something means to become curious or involved in it.

sentence: It's your turn to ___ care of the dog this weekend.
explanation: take care of somebody/something means to look after them.

sentence: He was sent to prison for ___ the law.
hint: collocation with 'the law' (opposite of obeying it)
explanation: break the law means to commit a crime; after the preposition 'for' the -ing form is needed.

sentence: The newspapers ___ the story about the minister's resignation.
hint: collocation with 'a story' meaning revealed it first
explanation: break a story is the journalism collocation meaning to be the first to report news.

sentence: She ___ the world record for the 100 metres last year.
explanation: break a record is the fixed collocation for performing better than the record.

sentence: It took him months to ___ the habit of biting his nails.
explanation: break a habit (or kick a habit) means to stop doing something you do regularly.

sentence: A sudden clap of thunder ___ the silence.
explanation: break the silence is the fixed collocation for ending a quiet period.

sentence: The referee warned the players not to ___ the rules.
hint: collocation with 'rules' (the referee warns against it)
explanation: break the rules means to disobey them; the context ('warned not to') requires this meaning.

sentence: Wrap up warm, or you'll ___ a cold.
explanation: catch a cold is the fixed collocation for becoming ill with one.

sentence: I was nearly late, but I managed to ___ the last bus.
hint: to get on a bus or train in time
explanation: catch a bus/train means to arrive in time to board it; the words 'managed to' and 'nearly late' show success.

sentence: The thief ran so fast that no one could ___ him.
hint: to capture someone who is running away
explanation: catch somebody means to capture or seize them after chasing.

sentence: The poster in the shop window ___ my eye.
explanation: catch somebody's eye means to attract someone's attention.

sentence: I only ___ sight of the celebrity for a second before the crowd closed in.
explanation: catch sight of somebody/something means to notice them briefly.

sentence: A true friend will always ___ a secret.
explanation: keep a secret is the fixed collocation for not telling it to anyone.

sentence: Despite the pressure, the surgeon ___ calm throughout the operation.
explanation: keep calm (or stay calm) means to remain calm; the past tense is needed here.

sentence: Even after she moved abroad, we ___ in touch by email.
explanation: keep in touch means to maintain contact with someone.

sentence: She has ___ a diary since she was twelve.
explanation: keep a diary is the fixed collocation for writing in one regularly.

sentence: You should ___ track of your spending.
explanation: keep track of something means to stay informed about it.

sentence: Unlike some politicians, she ___ her promises.
hint: collocation with 'promises' (she is unlike other politicians)
explanation: keep a promise means to do what you promised; the contrast with other politicians shows the positive verb.

sentence: The doctor has ___ detailed records of every patient since 1990.
explanation: keep records (of something) is the fixed collocation for storing information.

sentence: Try to ___ quiet — the exam is in progress.
explanation: keep quiet means to stay silent; 'make quiet' is not used.

sentence: Students should ___ attention when the teacher is speaking.
explanation: pay attention is the fixed collocation for listening or concentrating carefully.

sentence: He ___ her a compliment on her new hairstyle.
explanation: pay somebody a compliment is the fixed collocation for praising someone.

sentence: We ___ a visit to the museum while we were in Vienna.
explanation: pay a visit to somebody/something means to go and see them briefly.

sentence: We ___ a fortune for our new kitchen.
hint: fixed phrase: ___ a fortune for something
explanation: pay a fortune for something means to spend a very large amount buying it; the preposition 'for' follows 'pay'.

sentence: I'd rather ___ by card than carry cash.
explanation: pay by card/in cash is the fixed pattern for the method of payment.

sentence: The company ___ interest on the money it borrows.
explanation: pay interest is the standard financial collocation.

sentence: We stayed indoors because of the ___ rain.
explanation: heavy rain is the standard collocation; 'strong rain' is not used.

sentence: The ___ traffic added an hour to our journey.
explanation: heavy traffic means a lot of vehicles on the road; 'thick traffic' is not standard.

sentence: There was ___ fog at the airport all morning.
explanation: thick fog (or dense fog) is the standard collocation; 'strong fog' is wrong.

sentence: She has a ___ Scottish accent that is hard to miss.
explanation: a strong accent is the standard collocation; 'heavy accent' and 'deep accent' are not used.

sentence: Do you want a ___ cup of tea or a weak one?
explanation: strong tea/coffee means made with a lot of tea leaves or coffee; its opposite is weak.

sentence: The roads were almost empty — the traffic was surprisingly ___.
explanation: light traffic means few vehicles on the road; its opposite is heavy traffic.

sentence: Halfway through the film, the children were fast ___.
explanation: fast asleep means completely asleep; it is the fixed collocation with 'fast'.

sentence: It was three in the morning, but I was wide ___.
explanation: wide awake means completely awake; it is the fixed collocation with 'wide'.

sentence: Local residents are deeply ___ about the new motorway plan.
explanation: deeply concerned is the standard collocation meaning very worried; the other adjectives do not collocate with 'deeply'.

sentence: Make sure you are fully ___ of the terms before you sign.
explanation: fully aware of something is the fixed collocation meaning knowing completely.

sentence: Everyone agreed the suggestion was utterly ___.
explanation: utterly ridiculous is the standard collocation; 'utterly' is used with extreme adjectives.

sentence: I was slightly ___ by his rude reply.
explanation: slightly annoyed is a standard collocation; the other options are too strong to be 'slight'.

sentence: The crash left several passengers seriously ___.
explanation: seriously injured is the standard collocation describing bad injuries in accidents.

sentence: She was bitterly ___ when her proposal was rejected.
hint: adjective collocating with 'bitterly' after bad news
explanation: bitterly disappointed is the standard collocation; 'bitterly' combines with negative feelings.

sentence: It gets bitterly ___ here in January.
explanation: bitterly cold is the fixed collocation for extremely cold weather.

sentence: Our guide was highly ___ and had climbed the mountain five times.
explanation: highly experienced is the standard collocation; 'highly' combines with participial adjectives.

sentence: He was so badly ___ in the fall that he needed an operation.
explanation: badly hurt is the standard collocation meaning seriously injured.

sentence: We were deeply ___ by the news of the accident.
explanation: deeply shocked is the standard collocation for a strong negative reaction to news.

sentence: Her family has ___ a small hotel for thirty years.
hint: collocation with 'a hotel/business' meaning managed it
explanation: run a business/hotel means to manage or operate it; the past participle is needed after 'has'.

sentence: Ordering your food online can ___ you a lot of time.
explanation: save somebody time means to make it possible for them to use less time.

sentence: He ___ a fortune by buying his train ticket in advance.
explanation: save a fortune means to avoid spending a large amount; buying in advance keeps money.

sentence: I ___ hours yesterday trying to fix the printer, and it still doesn't work.
hint: fixed phrase: to use time without any result
explanation: waste time means to spend time uselessly; the second clause shows there was no result.

sentence: Stop ___ money on things you never use.
hint: to use money on useless things; -ing form after 'Stop'
explanation: waste money on something means to spend it on useless things; 'stop' is followed by the -ing form.

sentence: He always ___ the truth, however unpleasant it is.
explanation: tell the truth is the fixed collocation; 'say the truth' is a common learner error.

sentence: The boy knew it was wrong to ___ lies.
explanation: tell a lie / tell lies is the fixed collocation; a base verb is needed after 'to'.

sentence: Grandad's best man ___ a joke that made everyone laugh.
explanation: tell a joke is the fixed collocation; 'say a joke' is not used.

sentence: The children ___ us a long story about a dragon.
hint: collocation with 'a story' and a listener
explanation: tell somebody a story is the fixed pattern; 'say' and 'speak' do not take this pattern.

sentence: Most children learn to ___ the time before they start school.
hint: fixed phrase: ___ the time (read a clock)
explanation: tell the time means to be able to read a clock; it is a fixed expression.

sentence: After six hours of talks, the two sides finally ___ an agreement.
explanation: reach an agreement/decision is the collocation; 'arrive' would need 'at', which is not in the sentence.

sentence: The jury was unable to ___ a decision.
explanation: reach a decision is the fixed collocation; 'arrive' needs 'at' and cannot be followed directly by the object.

sentence: We ___ to the conclusion that the project was not viable.
explanation: come to the conclusion that ... is the fixed phrase; 'reach' and 'arrive' do not take 'to'.

sentence: If you ___ your word, people will trust you.
explanation: keep your word means to do what you promised.

sentence: Shall we split it, or will you ___ the bill?
explanation: pay the bill is the fixed collocation in restaurants; 'spend the bill' is wrong.

sentence: It was the manager's job to ___ the bad news to the staff.
hint: fixed phrase: ___ the news to somebody
explanation: break the news to somebody means to tell them something difficult or upsetting first.

sentence: My brother and I ___ turns washing up after dinner.
explanation: take turns means to do something one after another, alternating.

sentence: He ___ a speech at the wedding that moved everyone.
explanation: 'Make a speech' is the collocation; say/tell take different structures.

sentence: The judge ___ the verdict after four hours of deliberation.
explanation: 'Deliver a verdict/judgement' is the legal collocation.

sentence: We ___ the risk of flooding very seriously.
explanation: 'Take something seriously' is the fixed phrase.

sentence: She ___ attention to every detail of the contract.
explanation: 'Pay attention to' is the collocation.

sentence: The two sides struggled to ___ an agreement before the deadline.
explanation: 'Reach an agreement' = arrive at one.

sentence: It ___ no difference whether we leave today or tomorrow.
explanation: 'Make no difference' is the fixed phrase.

sentence: The critics ___ praise on the young violinist.
explanation: 'Heap praise on' = give a great deal of praise.

sentence: She ___ her breath before diving into the pool.
explanation: 'Hold one's breath' — catching breath is recovering it afterwards.

sentence: The company ___ losses of two million last year.
explanation: 'Report losses/profits' is the business collocation.

sentence: He ___ the blame for the accident onto the weather.
explanation: 'Shift the blame onto somebody' = transfer responsibility.

sentence: The children ___ great fun at the fair.
explanation: 'Have fun' — make/do do not collocate.

sentence: Their wedding ___ place on a remote island.
explanation: 'Take place' is the fixed phrase for events.

sentence: The company has ___ enormous losses this quarter.
explanation: 'Suffer losses' is the standard collocation for experiencing financial loss.

sentence: The ministry has ___ an inquiry into the collapse.
explanation: 'Order an inquiry' = officially commission a formal investigation.

sentence: Her talk really ___ home the urgency of the situation.
explanation: 'Drive something home' = make it fully understood.

sentence: The negotiators agreed to ___ the deadline by a fortnight.
explanation: 'Extend a deadline' = move it later; 'expand' means grow larger.

sentence: The new evidence has ___ doubt on the original conviction.
explanation: 'Throw doubt on' is the fixed phrase for casting suspicion on something.

sentence: The regulator has ___ its warning that the scheme may be unlawful.
explanation: 'Reiterate' = state again, formally; 'revoke' means cancel.

sentence: The judge ___ the jury to consider its verdict carefully.
explanation: 'Direct the jury' is the legal collocation for instructing it.

sentence: The charity ___ over a million euros in a single weekend appeal.
explanation: 'Raise money' takes an object; rise/rose/arose are intransitive.

sentence: The new CEO is keen to ___ her mark on the company.
hint: make your mark = have an impact
explanation: 'Make your mark on something' = have a clear, lasting effect on it.

sentence: The editors decided to ___ the chapter from the paperback edition.
explanation: "Omit" = leave out; the other -mit verbs mean let in, hand in, or send (money).

sentence: The company has ___ itself a reputation for ruthless efficiency.
explanation: 'Earn a reputation' = acquire it through behaviour over time.
